title: Common Legal Latin Terms
description: Latin phrases you'll meet in court opinions, law school, and the news, each with a literal translation and what it means in practice.
subject: law

cards.definition: "You shall have the body." A court order requiring that a detained person be brought before a judge to decide whether the detention is lawful.
"Guilty mind." The mental state, such as intent or recklessness, that the prosecution must prove for many crimes.
"The thing speaks for itself." Doctrine allowing negligence to be inferred when an accident normally wouldn't happen without it.
"Guilty act." The physical conduct, or unlawful failure to act, that makes up a crime.
"For the good," short for pro bono publico, "for the public good." Legal work done for free, usually for people or groups who can't afford a lawyer.
"For oneself." Representing yourself in a legal case without a lawyer.
"To stand by things decided." The principle that courts follow precedent set in earlier decisions.
"Friend of the court." Someone who isn't a party to a case but offers information or arguments, usually in a written brief.
"In good faith." Genuine and sincere, without intent to deceive.
"In fact." Existing in practice, whether or not it is officially or legally recognized.
"By law." Existing by legal right or official recognition.
"After the fact." Describes a law applied retroactively; the U.S. Constitution bars ex post facto criminal laws.
"At first sight." Evidence strong enough to establish a fact or claim unless it is rebutted.
"A matter judged." Rule that a claim decided on the merits can't be relitigated between the same parties.
"By the court." An opinion issued in the name of the court as a whole rather than signed by a particular judge.
"In chambers." Proceedings or review held in private, such as in a judge's chambers, away from the public.
"To be made more certain." A writ by which a higher court, such as the U.S. Supreme Court, agrees to review a lower court's decision.
"Under penalty." A legal order requiring a person to testify or produce documents, with penalties for refusing.
"Let the buyer beware." The principle that a buyer is responsible for checking the quality of goods before purchase.
"Something for something." An exchange in which one thing is given in return for another.
"Of its own accord." Action a court takes on its own initiative, without a request from either party.
"Beyond the powers." Acts taken beyond the legal authority of a person, government body, or corporation.
"I do not wish to contend." A no-contest plea in which a defendant accepts punishment without admitting guilt.
"In the place of a parent." Taking on some of a parent's legal responsibilities, as schools may for students.
